paragraphs.text: Red Edge oolong from Nantou, Taiwan, made in 2024. The name records how it was made: the edges of each leaf were left to oxidise further until they turned red, while the centre of the leaf stayed green.

That puts both ends of [oolong](oolong:definition) in a single leaf, the type that stands between green tea, which is not oxidised, and red tea, which is oxidised all the way. It belongs to [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition), whose plants and craft came to the island from Fujian, and it is rolled, as most of the island's oolong is.

At two years it is a young tea. Taiwan keeps some oolong for many years as [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea, and those who give a figure for when an oolong counts as old put it somewhere between ten and thirty years.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: In light high mountain tea: a sweet, floral cup, often creamy or buttery, with little bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste. In roasted Dong Ding: caramel, ripe fruit, nuts and a toasted aroma. In Baozhong: floral notes and a clear, bright liquor. In Oriental Beauty: ripe fruit and honey, with little bitterness.
